Parvaim
pär-vā'im
n. (the place whose gold garnished the house Solomon built, named once only in Scripture)
From Hebrew Parvayim, of unknown site; the dual ending has suggested to some an Arabian district of two parts, and to others a general term for gold of a particular refinement. It occurs one time in the whole Bible, at the building of the temple.

Biblical Definition

Parvaim is a single word in a single verse, and everything about it belongs to the house of the LORD. The Chronicler is describing the finishing of the most holy place, and interrupts a list of measurements to name the source of the metal: “And he garnished the house with precious stones for beauty: and the gold was gold of Parvaim” (2Ch 3:6). Kings records the same work from the other side, without the place-name but with the totality: “And the whole house he overlaid with gold, until he had finished all the house: also the whole altar that was by the oracle he overlaid with gold” (1Ki 6:22). The temple was not gilded in patches. Floor, walls, doors, the partition of chains before the oracle, the altar — all overlaid, and studded with precious stones, and where the finest of that gold came from, the Chronicler tells us. He does not tell us where Parvaim was, and the site has never been recovered. That is worth noticing about a book often accused of embroidering: a writer inventing splendour has no reason to invent an obscure and unexplained proper noun. He records it because it was in the record, the way a builder's account names a quarry.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Parvaim; in sacred history it is the place whence came the gold with which Solomon garnished the house of the LORD.

expand to see more

PARVAIM, n. A place named once in the Scriptures, in the second book of Chronicles.

The gold with which Solomon garnished the house was gold of Parvaim.

The situation of the place is wholly unknown to us.

Some have supposed it a district of Arabia, and others a term of quality in gold.

The whole house, floor, walls and doors, was overlaid with gold, and set with precious stones for beauty.

Key Scripture

2Ch 3:6 — "And he garnished the house with precious stones for beauty: and the gold was gold of Parvaim."

1Ki 6:21 — "So Solomon overlaid the house within with pure gold: and he made a partition by the chains of gold before the oracle; and he overlaid it with gold."

1Ki 6:22 — "And the whole house he overlaid with gold, until he had finished all the house: also the whole altar that was by the oracle he overlaid with gold."

2Ch 3:8 — "And he made the most holy house, the length whereof was according to the breadth of the house, twenty cubits, and the breadth thereof twenty cubits: and he overlaid it with fine gold, amounting to six hundred talents."

Modern Corruption

There is no significant modern redefinition of this place. The principle to recover is that God commanded costly beauty in His own worship, and that the regulative principle governs the manner of worship without requiring meanness in it.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Parvaim is a gold source named once and nobody has contested it. What the verse sets against a certain strain of piety is the fact that God Himself specified expense. The gold of the most holy place was not the extravagance of a king indulging himself; the pattern came from the LORD by the hand of David, and the Chronicler weighs the gold to six hundred talents (2Ch 3:8). Beauty in the worship of God is commanded, not merely tolerated, and the tabernacle before it was the same — blue, purple, scarlet, fine twined linen, cunning work, and men filled with the Spirit of God to do it.

The principle to recover holds two things together that are often set at odds. Worship is governed by the regulative principle: what God has commanded is required, what He has not commanded is not permitted, and no man may add a ceremony because he finds it moving. But within what He commands, He has never asked for shabbiness. The same Scripture that forbids will-worship records six hundred talents of the gold of Parvaim on the walls of the oracle. A congregation may meet in a plain room and worship rightly; what it may not do is conclude that carelessness is humility, or that God is honoured by giving Him the leavings.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Parvayim (H6516), Parvaim; chaphah (H2645), to overlay, cover; debiyr (H1687), oracle, the innermost sanctuary; 'eben yeqarah (H68 with H3368), precious stone; kikkar (H3603), talent.

expand to see more

Hebrew Parvayim (H6516) — Parvaim; named once, for the gold of the temple.

Hebrew chaphah (H2645) — to overlay; the verb of the whole gilding.

Hebrew debiyr (H1687) — the oracle; the most holy place within.

Hebrew 'eben (H68) — stone; with yaqar, the precious stones for beauty.

Hebrew kikkar (H3603) — talent; six hundred of them in gold.

Usage

"“The gold was gold of Parvaim” — a quarry named in a builder's account."

"“He garnished the house with precious stones for beauty” — beauty as a stated purpose."

"“Until he had finished all the house” — nothing left unoverlaid."
